entry.title: Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Exactly Once In Order routing for XI and IDoc inbound processing
entry.content:
In the newest version of the Pipeline for Cloud Integration, we added Exactly Once In Order (EOIO) routing directly into the inbound processing step for both XI and IDoc — the two protocols where ordered delivery matters most in SAP-to-SAP integration. When a message arrives flagged as EOIO, the pipeline detects this at the earliest possible stage and routes it on a dedicated route — bypassing the pipeline steps that are currently incompatible with ordered processing today — and forwards it either to an exclusive JMS queue or a ProcessDirect endpoint. See In Order Handling.

It was a conscious decision not to support EOIO in the pipeline right now as long as we do not support dynamic serialization context which - once supported - will give us much more flexibility in handling EOIO scenarios. So, the current delivery does not cover an End-to-End scenario for EOIO but is a first step to unblock customers that are requiring this and want to use the generic IDoc and Proxy inbound.

You configure the EOIO routes in the Partner Directory for the partner ID representing your configuration scenario. For this, the string parameter InOrderRouteOption has been introduced. As value of the parameter, you need to specify the route option and its specifics. The following options are supported:

  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue which name is based on the sender context.
  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue with a name chosen in the Partner Directory.
  • You route the EOIO messages to a ProcessDirect endpoint.

If nothing has been configured, EOIO messages will fail in the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with custom status ConfigurationOptionNotSupported.

In either case, you need to create an integration flow where you implement the In Order settings on your own. For the ProcessDirect option, you directly send the EOIO message synchronously to the integration flow. When choosing the exclusive queue option, you decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows from your integration flow. By persisting the messages in a JMS queue, Cloud Integration can carry out the retry of the message delivery if there's an error. Because an exclusive JMS queue can have only one consumer at a time, the message sequence can be preserved. See Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order.

In the following, let's go through the different options.

Exclusive queue based on sender context

For XI messages sent with Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order, the XI sender adapter sets the message headers SapQualityOfService equals ExactlyOnceInOrder and SapQueueId holding the queue ID of the incoming message. For the IDoc sender adapter, the message headers SapPlainSoapQoS and SapPlainSoapQueueId are set based on the IDoc control header ARCKEY. Your EOIO messages can then be routed to an exclusive queue with a name provided in the headers SapQueueId and SapPlainSoapQueueId, respectively.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the name of the queue ID sent with the message. If different queue IDs are sent, you need to create multiple integration flows. As you can see, this doesn't scale unlimited. So, this only works for quite static queue settings.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:UseSenderContextAsQueue.

Exclusive queue with configured name

Like in the option before, you can use an exclusive JMS queue to decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with from your integration flow. Here, however, you can give the exclusive queue an own name.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the configured name, here PIP2EOIO, see below.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:<your chosen queue name>, in this example ExclusiveQueue:PIP2EOIO.

Optionally, because we bypass the rest of the pipeline, in particular the receiver determination, you can create a string parameter receiverDetermination with value equals the receiver system name. Another option would be to create a message header SAP_Receiver in the integration flow holding the receiver system name. This is actually supported for all options, but not shown in the other screenshots.

ProcessDirect option

You can route the EOIO message to an integration flow which you synchronously call via ProcessDirect adapter. In this case, create an integration flow with a ProcessDirect sender adapter.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ProcessDirect:<your chosen ProcessDirect end point>, in this example ProcessDirect:/PIP/Step07/Samples/Scenario_2/EOIO.

 

Special use case: XI to XI route-through

Let's take a look at a special use case. We like to achieve EOIO delivery for a route-through scenario with XI sender and XI receiver, i.e., Point-to-Point without mapping. In this case, we can actually apply the ProcessDirect option whereas as ProcessDirect In Order route we choose the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. So, the generic XI inbound processing flow directly calls the generic XI outbound processing flow. The headers SapQualityOfService and SapQueueId are passed through. This ensures that the XI receiver adapter calls the receiver system in Exactly Once In Order mode. Furthermore, dynamic queue IDs are supported. Note, that in this case, the restart in case of a message failure is handled by the sender system.

In the following, we go through the configuration in detail. The colour coding is defined as follows: Green has to do with the landscape staging settings and the partner ID determination, Blue refers to the In Order routing, and Red refers to the XI outbound settings. First of all, we need a partner ID representing the sender system alias with an alternative partner that maps the actual sender business system to the sender system alias. In this case, we assume that we run the scenario in the QA landscape. For an incoming message, the business system is mapped to the alias. Within the pipeline, we work with alias.

Next, for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario we define an alternative partner that maps the sender system alias, the sender interface name and the sender interface namespace to the configuration scenario. This way, we determine the configuration scenario based on the incoming message.

On the String Parameters tab, we define how the configuration scenario is configured. The string parameter receiverDetermination defines the receiver system alias. The InOrderRouteOption defines how we handle the In Order processing. In this case, we opt for the ProcessDirect option. As mentioned above, as address we maintain the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. Furthermore, we define the settings of the XI outbound processing, in this case the receiver interface name and its namespace. See XI Receiver Adapter.

For the receiver system alias, we also need to define an alternative partner that maps the actual receiver business system to the receiver system alias. Before we send out the message to the receiver, we map the alias to the corresponding business system.

For configuring the XI connection parameters, we support different options. In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For this, we create a partner ID representing the actual receiver business system and maintain the configuration parameters. i.e., proxy type, authentication type, credential name, and XI end point of the receiver system. For a complete list of configuration options, see XI Receiver Adapter.

If you run the scenario, you should see two message processing logs in the message monitor belonging to one message exchange. As you can see, the message has been routed through and delivered via Exactly Once In Order.

The options outlined here are initial steps to realize EOIO extending the generic XI and IDoc pipeline steps. We are looking into options to realize the E2E scenario using Exclusive Queue but also the planned "Support many serialization contexts for parallel exactly once in order processing (EOIO)" via the pipeline. Therefore, please stay tuned for further updates of the pipeline package.

we have our own app built on top of SAP BTP ABAP Environment.  The solution has own namespace e.g. /NS/ and it generates various application logs for our own application log objects like /NS/EXPORT. We want to provide own app where users can see individual application logs. We followed the following tutorial how to define own application log app using adaptation project. 

https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/how-to-create-standalone-application-logs-tile

The app works fine when executed locally. When we try to deploy it as an app /NS/LOG, we get the following error during deployment.

The app uses not permitted services for ABAP for Cloud Development

We looked at the details of the message and the problem seems to be that our package is /NS/LOG is ABAP for Cloud Development (it must be) but the application log service has not been released for consumption. 

How are we supposed to deliver an app that users could use to preview application logs? There does not seem to be a generic app that could be used on SAP BTP ABAP Environment? Ironically, I was able to teach Claude Code to read the messages directly from the service without any issues.

entry.title: SAP-managed Public Cloud ERP: Accelerating the Path to the Autonomous Enterprise
entry.content:
This blog is co-authored by Stephan Hetzer, Thomas Bieser, Daniel Kesenheimer, and Neetin Datar.

Somewhere Along the Way, Simplicity Gave Way to Complexity

For decades, ERP has been designed to simplify enterprise management and operations. Yet as organizations adopted cloud applications and best-of-breed line-of-business (LoB) solutions, complexity often grew alongside innovation. Customers increasingly found themselves managing heterogeneous application landscapes, custom integrations, workflows, security models, and operational dependencies.

The irony is striking. Organizations moved to the cloud expecting simplicity, but many discovered that managing enterprise software had become a significant undertaking:

  • Implementation teams became integration teams
  • Business transformation programs became technology orchestration programs

As a result, time-to-value stretched, organizations spent more time managing technology and less time realizing business outcomes.

Business leaders want outcomes, not infrastructure. Yet for many organizations, managing the software became the problem.

Why This Matters More Than Ever

Historically, organizations could tolerate this complexity because ERP systems primarily functioned as systems of record.

That is no longer enough.

The rise of AI assistants, AI agents, and autonomous business processes is fundamentally changing what organizations expect from enterprise software.

AI does not operate within organizational silos. For example, an AI assistant helping a manager make workforce decisions may need information from HR, finance, procurement, operations, and company policies simultaneously. Likewise, autonomous business processes must flow seamlessly across organizational boundaries.

This creates a new requirement for enterprise software.

Integration Alone Is No Longer Sufficient

For years, enterprise software has focused on helping systems exchange data. In the age of Business AI, systems must do more than that. They must share business meaning, context, and process understanding. The distinction is important:

  • Technical interoperability enables systems to communicate.
  • Semantic interoperability enables systems to collaborate.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in business processes, the organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most AI models. They will be those with the most connected business processes, enabled by both technical and semantic interoperability.

The Autonomous Enterprise Era

Today, we are in a new era. It is the era of the Autonomous Enterprise.

Organizations increasingly expect enterprise systems to be:

  • AI-ready by design, built on harmonized and trusted data, connected business processes, a shared semantic layer, and strong governance that allow AI assistants and agents to operate in a business context
  • End-to-end integrated
  • Continuously updated
  • Operationally simple

The expectation is shifting from managing software to consuming business capability.

This shift is foundational for the Autonomous Enterprise. In an Autonomous Enterprise, real-time data, embedded business AI, deep process knowledge, and strong governance work together to enable greater speed, simplicity, and resilience.

Our recent customer experiences are beginning to demonstrate what it looks like in practice.

Surprising Early Results

With the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2602 release, SAP introduced the SAP-managed Workforce Management business process, which integrates SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. It was made available to selected customers.

Early customer experience delivered compelling results:

  • Provisioning a single integrated landscape for both applications was completed in 1 business day, including all Core Foundational Services such as Identity and Access Management.
  • The technical integration took only about 15 minutes.

Anyone who has participated in enterprise software implementation will immediately recognize the significance of these results. Customers and implementation partners also report benefits from the out-of-the-box, business-driven activation of SAP-managed scenarios, which dramatically reduces time-to-value and landscape complexity. Tasks that traditionally required extensive coordination across provisioning, onboarding, security, integration, and testing are significantly streamlined, reducing effort from weeks and days to hours and minutes.

The significance lies not in the results themselves, but in what they represent: a future in which customers spend less time assembling enterprise systems and more time transforming their businesses.

SAP's Bold Move

These industry dynamics are driving SAP's move toward SAP-managed public cloud ERP (1).

Historically, customers and their implementation partners carried responsibility for managing the entire software lifecycle, including provisioning, identity and access management, technical integration, configuration, and ongoing maintenance.

With SAP-managed public cloud ERP, SAP manages key technical and operational aspects of the solution, including provisioning, technical integration, monitoring, automatic updates, backups, and offboarding. Rather than requiring customers and partners to assemble and operate the digital foundation, SAP manages core lifecycle and operational services, enabling them to focus on business outcomes.

Note: Business process design and configuration, data management, testing, user adoption, organizational readiness, and other implementation activities remain essential and continue to be managed by customers and their implementation partners.

This shift to SAP-managed does not diminish the importance of implementation partners. Rather, it further enhances it. Partners can now focus more deeply on business transformation, process innovation, industry expertise, change management, and value realization. With reduced integration variability and operational complexity, partners can also deliver more predictable outcomes and help customers accelerate time-to-value.

Just as cloud computing abstracted much of the complexity of infrastructure management, SAP-managed public cloud ERP seeks to reduce the setup and operational complexity of running enterprise applications, while accelerating time-to-value.

This is more than an operational improvement. It represents a shift in how ERP is delivered, consumed, and ultimately valued.

In many ways, it aligns directly with SAP's goal to help customers become Autonomous Enterprises.

What's Available Today as SAP-Managed

SAP’s initial focus is on high-value, cross-functional business processes where customers can benefit immediately from pre-integrated operations and simplified lifecycle management.

Current SAP-managed offerings include:

  • Workforce Management for organizations implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition together with SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central
  • Operational Procurement for organizations running SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition with SAP Ariba Buying and SAP Ariba Invoicing
  • Opportunity-to-Order for organizations implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition together with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2

Over time, SAP plans to expand managed capabilities across additional business processes and solution areas.

Call to Action: Join the Early Adoption Care (EAC) Program

For organizations implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition alongside SAP SuccessFactors, SAP Ariba, or SAP Sales Cloud Version 2, the EAC program offers a unique opportunity to explore the SAP-managed approach.

Participants gain early access to innovation, direct engagement with SAP experts, and the opportunity to provide feedback based on real-world implementation experiences. They can help shape the future of SAP-managed public cloud ERP in a meaningful way.

Find more information and register for the EAC programs here:

  • Customer Influence Portal for SAP-managed Workforce Management
  • Customer Influence Portal for SAP-managed Opportunity to Order
  • Customer Influence Portal for SAP-managed Operational Procurement

From Managing Software to Consuming Business Capabilities

The significance of SAP-managed public cloud ERP extends beyond automated system setup, reduced operational complexity, and faster time-to-value.

The bigger story is the continued evolution of ERP itself, from a system of record to a foundation for intelligent, increasingly autonomous business processes.

As AI assistants, AI agents, and autonomous business processes become increasingly embedded in day-to-day operations, organizations will need enterprise systems that are connected, context-aware, and operationally simple.

SAP-managed public cloud ERP helps build that foundation. Just as cloud computing transformed how organizations consumed infrastructure, SAP-managed public cloud ERP is helping transform how they consume enterprise software.

Ultimately, the future of ERP is not about managing applications. It is about enabling intelligent, connected, and increasingly autonomous enterprises.

As Business AI continues to evolve, the organizations that thrive will be those that spend less time managing technology and more time creating business value.

entry.title: SmartRecruiters and OpenText via SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
Introduction

Many SAP SuccessFactors customers use OpenText as their document management system, integrated with Employee Central (EC) and Onboarding. When these same customers adopt SmartRecruiters (SR) as their ATS, a common question arises:

"Can candidate documents from SmartRecruiters be pushed to OpenText — just like documents from EC and Onboarding?"

The short answer: Yes — and here's how.

How It Works: The Core Principle

  • OpenText remains enabled for EC and Onboarding customers — it does not get disabled when SmartRecruiters is in use.
  • SmartRecruiters uses its own storage for candidate documents.
  • The integration extracts attachments from SmartRecruiters and inserts them into Onboarding or EC. Once inserted into SuccessFactors, the documents flow automatically to OpenText.

Document Types in SmartRecruiters

#

Document Type

Description

1

Candidate Attachments

Documents uploaded during the application (e.g., payslips, ID proofs)

2

Resume

Uploaded when the candidate creates their profile

3

Offer Letter

Offer letter sent to the candidate

4

Offer Attachments

Policy documents or attachments added to the offer

Document types 1 & 2 are available via standard API (Out of the box)

Document types 3 & 4 (offer letters and attachments) are supported only if the offer was sent via DocuSign.

It is important to note that this is a complex integration scenario. The content presented here offers a general architectural approach to help customers navigate a custom integration path. Each implementation will differ based on specific process designs and business requirements — additional custom logic, MDF objects, RBP configurations, API calls, and Integration Suite capabilities may be necessary. We strongly recommend conducting a proof of concept (POC).

 

Integration Design: Step-by-Step Flow

Step1: Initiate Onboarding from SmartRecruiters

Hire the candidate in SmartRecruiters and initiate Onboarding. This creates an onboarding external user in SuccessFactors and triggers an Intelligent Service Center (ISC) event. Consume the ISC event from SF (not from SR). This confirms that the SF user has been created and event is created with a reference to SmartRecruiters application ID (SR_Application_ID).

SAP Engineering has implemented a field mapping to support this:

Onboarding Source

Field Populated

SmartRecruiters

SR_Application_ID

RCM

ATS_Application_ID

The SR_Application_ID field creates a unique link between the SR candidate and the SF user.

ISC event triggered on the SuccessFactors side: “Onboarding is initiated from an external Applicant Tracking System”.

Step 2: Extract attachments for the candidate from SmartRecruiters using application ID.

Screen shot of attachments stored on the candidate:

To pull attachments from the candidate, use API – https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/reference/candidatesattachmentslist-1

Example:

Sample Request and response –

Get call – https://api.smartrecruiters.com/candidates/f912005a-37da-4672-b06d-409dac0d39f0/attachments

For offer letters we have similar API query to extract offer documents- refer to the query below: (Works only with Docusign enabled): https://api.smartrecruiters.com/candidates/{id}/jobs/{jobId}/offers

Step 3: Check OpenText integration settings in Successfactors 

  • Admin Tools -> Configure Document Management -> OpenText should be selected.
  • When OpenText integration is enabled: Documents are physically stored in OpenText, but SuccessFactors still manages the attachment metadata layer.
  • The SuccessFactors Attachment OData entity remains the API access point
  • attachmentId is still the business key returned in the API response, e.g.: { "d": [ { "key": "Attachment/attachmentId=499", "status": "OK", ... } ] }
  • Document categories should be configured to map documents to corresponding OpenText folders.

Step 4: Review the behavior of attachment API

Use Successfactors Attachment API to insert attachments and generate a unique Attachment ID for each of the documents. Maintain mapping of all documents to their respective attachment ID’s.

Attachment API: https://help.sap.com/docs/successfactors-platform/sap-successfactors-api-reference-guide-odata-v2/attachment

To link attachments to custom MDF objects: https://help.sap.com/docs/successfactors-platform/sap-successfactors-api-reference-guide-odata-v2/linking-attachments-to-mdf-entity

Step 5: Insert attachments to custom MDF objects in Onboarding or Employee Central.

5.1 Onboarding

Create a custom MDF object with attachment fields to store the documents and associate with ONB 2.0 Additional Data Collection Step. The steps are documented in another community blog (credits to Sumanan_Sivan) https://community.sap.com/t5/human-capital-management-blog-posts-by-members/integrating-attachments-from-custom-data-collection-object-to-onboarding/ba-p/13583427 . This blog specifically covers the scenario where candidates upload attachments in the UI. You can replace that step with the use of the Attachment API & custom MDF object APIs.

5.2 Employee Central

Create a custom MDF object with attachment fields to store the documents.

Create a Custom Card to display MDF object data on the latest people profile: https://help.sap.com/docs/successfactors-platform/configuring-people-profile/custom-cards

Leverage the Attachment API & custom MDF object APIs to insert attachments and to display on the custom card.

When the Onboarding module is not in use, the flow starts differently — consume the new Employee Hire event in Step 1 and proceed with the remaining steps accordingly.

I hope this was helpful — feel free to share your thoughts or questions in the comments below.

entry.title: Step-by-Step installing EWM Outbound Value Accelerator for SAP Signavio Process Intelligence

Warehouse labor costs are rising, OTIF (On-Time In-Full) performance is under pressure, and transformation budgets are being scrutinized harder than ever.

If you are running embedded SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) and have access to SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, you are just a few steps away from deep visibility into your outbound warehouse processes — without writing a single query.

This post is the written companion to our hands-on webcast and walks SCM process analysts and warehouse transformation leaders through the complete installation of the Identify Improvement Potential for embedded SAP Extended Warehouse Management (Outbound) (Pipeline) and Improve Process Performance for embedded Warehouse Management (Outbound)  (Analytical Dashboards) value accelerator packages, step by step, with annotated screenshots.

If you missed the live session — or want to revisit the steps — the full webcast recording is available here. At the end you will find links to additional resources, dashboards, and connectivity documentation.

What the EWM Value Accelerator Delivers

The accelerator provides a pre-built data transformation pipeline and a set of dashboards covering:

  • On-time delivery performance — track whether warehouse outbound tasks are completed within the promised time windows
  • Warehouse operation KPIs — cycle times, throughput, bottleneck identification
  • Process improvement opportunities — variant analysis and conformance gaps in the Plan-to-Fulfill process

It is published by SAP, works with SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, and targets SAP Extended Warehouse Management source systems.

Prerequisites

  • Access to an SAP Signavio Process Intelligence workspace
  • A data connector established between SAP Signavio Process Intelligence and your SAP EWM source system (RFC extractor or manual CSV upload)
  • Permissions to install accelerators in your workspace

Step-by-Step Installation Guide

Steps 1 & 2 — Open the Value Accelerator Library

Expand the left navigation panel (1) and click Value Accelerator Library under Browse and Manage (2).

 

Steps 3 & 4 — Search for the EWM Accelerator and Select It

Use the search box (3) and enter:
"Identify Improvement Potential for embedded SAP Extended Warehouse Management (Outbound)"
Then select the accelerator card from the results (4).

 

Steps 5 & 6 — Review the Accelerator Details and Install

Click Install the value accelerator (5). Review the metadata (6) and confirm it matches your setup:

  • Product & License: SAP Signavio Process Intelligence
  • Process: Plan-to-Fulfill
  • System: SAP Extended Warehouse Management
  • Content: Dashboards + Data Pipeline
  • Line of Business: Supply Chain
  • Value Driver: Improve on-time delivery

Click OK to confirm the installation.

 

 

Steps 7–9 — Configure a New Analysis Configuration

Select "Install accelerator in a new analysis configuration" (7). Click Review (8), check the summary, then click Finish (9) to start the installation.

 

Installation Status

After clicking Finish, you are redirected to a status page. Wait for the installation to complete.

 

Steps 10 & 11 — Navigate to Data Management

Open the left panel (10) and navigate to Data Management (11) under Mine and Analyze.

 

Steps 12–14 — Find and Sort the Created Pipeline

Click the double-arrow sort icon (12), sort by Created date descending (13), and click OK. Select the newly created EWM pipeline (14).

 

Steps 15–18 — Link the Data Connection to the Pipeline

Click Add a data connection (15). Search for your existing data connector (16), click on it (17), then click Link (18).

 

Step 19 — Run the ETL Pipeline

Click Run ETL (19) to extract, transform, and load data from your source system.

Tip: Choose Run ETL if you have not yet extracted data (using the RFC extractor). Choose Run T&L (Transform & Load only) if you have already extracted data or are using manual CSV uploads.

 

Step 20 — Open the Analysis Configuration

Once the pipeline completes, click the analysis configuration box (20) to navigate to the installed dashboards.

 

Step 21 — Open the Dashboard

Click on any dashboard tile (21) to enter the analysis and start exploring your EWM outbound process data.

 

Congratulations — Your EWM Analytics Are Live!

You have successfully installed the SAP EWM Value Accelerator. You now have pre-built dashboards covering on-time delivery, throughput, and process improvement opportunities in your outbound warehouse process.

entry.title: Part 2 : SAP Datasphere: High-Level Overview
entry.content:
Hello All,

Previous Post: Part 1: SAP Business Data Cloud an overview - SAP Community

In this blog, I will provide an overview of SAP Datasphere, exploring its key capabilities, core components, and how organizations can get started with the platform.

The following diagram presents a high-level architectural view of SAP Datasphere, highlighting the core services, data flows, and integration capabilities within the platform.

 

 

What Is a Space?

A Space is a secure and isolated workspace within SAP Datasphere where users can connect, prepare, model, and manage data. Created and administered by tenant administrators, spaces are typically designed for specific business units, departments, projects, data domains, or teams.

Think of a space as a dedicated data warehouse environment running on SAP HANA Cloud, complete with its own resources, users, and data assets. All data acquisition, transformation, and modeling activities in SAP Datasphere take place within a space, ensuring clear separation, governance, and security.

By design, data remains confined to its originating space and cannot be accessed from other spaces unless it is intentionally shared or exposed for consumption. This controlled approach enables organizations to manage data ownership while promoting trusted collaboration across different teams and business functions.

Types of Spaces in SAP Datasphere

Standard Space

 A Standard Space is the default and mandatory space type in SAP Datasphere, designed for common data acquisition, preparation, transformation, and modeling activities. Administrators can create and configure multiple standard spaces to support different business units, projects, or data domains.

This space type provides maximum flexibility with no inherent restrictions. Administrators can create, modify, and delete spaces as needed, while authorized users can freely create, manage, and maintain data objects within their assigned spaces.

Standard Spaces can leverage either the SAP HANA Cloud Database (disk-based and in-memory storage) or SAP HANA Data Lake Files, enabling organizations to choose the storage option that best meets their performance, scalability, and data retention requirements.

Data Lake Space

A Data Lake Space is designed for ingesting, storing, and preparing large volumes of data in a cost-effective staging environment. Unlike standard spaces, data in a Data Lake Space is stored in the SAP Datasphere Object Store, making it well suited for handling high data volumes at a lower storage cost.

This space type supports a limited set of connectivity options and is primarily intended for replication-based data ingestion through replication flows. To enable Data Lake Spaces, administrators must allocate object store resources in the tenant configuration, with a minimum requirement of 128 GB of memory.

Data processing and transformation activities in a Data Lake Space are powered by Apache Spark, which serves as the primary execution engine for data preparation and transformation workflows. The underlying storage layer for this space type is SAP HANA Data Lake Files, providing scalable and efficient storage for large datasets.

Views

Once you deploy the space, you can start building your views and bring in data using the appropriate connections to your source systems.

The image above provides an overview of the supported connection types that can be used to connect to source systems.

It is important to understand the requirements for sharing data products on Databricks. Data products cannot be published from Disk and In-Memory Space. Only data stored in the SAP HANA Lake Files Space is eligible for publication as a data product.

While data products cannot be published directly from Disk and In-Memory Space, you can always share views from these spaces with the SAP HANA Lake Files Space.

For better understanding, I’ve included a graphical representation below that illustrates how data products are shared and published.

 

This provides a high-level overview of SAP Datasphere and how the overall platform works.
 
Going forward, I’ll dive deeper into how connections work in SAP Datasphere, how data is pulled from different source systems, and which connection types are most commonly used, such as SAP ECC, ABAP, SAP HANA, SQL-based systems, and SAP SuccessFactors.
 
Thank you
Yogesh

entry.title: Integration Advisor – RosettaNet PIP Messages
entry.content:
I am happy to share the latest update to the B2B offerings of Integration Advisor and Cloud Integration (part of SAP Integration Suite): the RosettaNet Message Standard is now supported. In this blog post, I will give you a brief overview of this message standard and explain how to use it.

RosettaNet Library in Integration Advisor

This new B2B library consists of the so-called RosettaNet Partner Interface Processes (PIPs), specified for the high-tech industry. This standard was originally owned by the RosettaNet consortium and later became part of the GS1 US organization.

Our offering includes a total of 269 messages across 104 distinct PIP codes. See the screenshot below for an example of the Messages list in Integration Advisor.

Our content is based on the original RosettaNet specifications previously published on the GS1 US website. Note that this content was removed from the GS1 US webpage earlier in 2026.

More specifically, we considered the PIP specifications for the 01, 02, and 03 version series. RosettaNet had also begun converting some of the PIP specifications into a newer XSD-based format, published as the V11 series. The content of this V11 series is currently not available in Integration Advisor, as it was not part of SAP Process Integration and SAP Process Orchestration (SAP PI/PO) and we have not received any reports of customers using this newer format. Please contact us (e.g. via a comment on this blog post) if you require the V11 series. Based on demand, we can add it to Integration Advisor at a later stage.

One additional background note: RosettaNet distinguishes between the following version status types for a PIP version: Draft (D) → Beta (B) → Release (R) → Validated (V), where V represents the final state. The majority of the offered PIPs (216) are in the Validated state (e.g. PIP3A4_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest). In addition, GS1 US listed a number of PIPs (53) in the Released state (e.g. PIP2C7_R01_00_BillOfMaterialConfirmation). Based on our interpretation, these PIPs were released and used productively but were never advanced to the final Validated state, and were therefore listed with their last known status. For two specific PIPs (PIP2C9 and PIP3B11) GS1 US listed content for both R and V states, and we have followed this approach in Integration Advisor. Please note that no content considered work-in-progress (i.e. Draft or Beta states) is offered.

Versioning of RosettaNet Messages

RosettaNet versioned all messages separately and published updates for each message independently. This means there is no concept comparable to a release version as known from many other B2B standards (such as 004010 for ASC X12, D.01B for UN/EDIFACT, or 1.2.065 for cXML). 

For example, in the screenshot above, PIP3A4_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest represents version V02.02 of the PurchaseOrderRequest message (PIP code PIP3A4). For some message types, multiple versions were published (e.g. 9 versions for PIP4C1 or 7 versions for PIP3A4), while other message types have only a single version (e.g. PIP3A13 or PIP4A1). 

Due to this versioning strategy, and given that no further updates to RosettaNet messages are expected, all definitions are grouped in Integration Advisor into a single version called All. This version contains 267 message types. 

Moreover, the RosettaNet standard didn't define reusable Codelists, Complex Types, or Simple Types. Therefore, no explicit content is provided in the corresponding sections in Integration Advisor. However, the Codelists, Complex Types, and Simple Types are implicitly part of the RosettaNet message types and frequently exhibit similar details across different message types.

Additional Semantic Details for RosettaNet Messages

In Integration Advisor, we always strive to go beyond the pure technical specification of a B2B library. We provide additional semantic details inline and out of the box. These include, for example, documentation, allowed code values, and value specifications (via data type, length, and representation).

The RosettaNet standard technically specified the RosettaNet PIP messages based on the older schema definition language DTD. Such DTDs do not include additional semantic details such as documentation or value specifications. All values are assumed to be of type String, and no length information is available. This is why other mapping tools such as SAP Process Integration and SAP Process Orchestration (SAP PI/PO) do not offer semantic details for RosettaNet.

In addition, RosettaNet published so-called Message Guidelines (in HTML format), which included more semantic details such as documentation, code values with descriptions, and details for Simple Types including length and representation.

In the Integration Advisor offering, the technical DTD specification and the semantic HTML guideline details are combined to provide a holistic view of all the details of a RosettaNet PIP message. For an example, see the screenshot below.

Besides adding semantic details, the RosettaNet HTML guidelines also permit certain deviations from the actual message structure, such as deselecting optional elements or restricting cardinality. When preparing the content for Integration Advisor, we decided to keep the PIP message structure in line with the technical DTD specification and to use the HTML guidelines solely for enriching semantic details.

Special attention was given to the appropriate representation of data types and their properties. The following table provides more details on how the RosettaNet data types are represented in Integration Advisor.

RosettaNet used the concept of Representation to further specify the allowed value space. For example, the representation 9(9)4(X) (for Global Location Identifier) means that (up to) 9 digits are followed by (up to) 4 characters (e.g. 123456789ZZZ). In Integration Advisor, the Representation (where specified by RosettaNet) can be found in the details area for a node, under the Notes tab.

A few things to note regarding the representation of three Global Identifiers in the RosettaNet content:

  • Global Business Identifier
    • The GlobalBusinessIdentifieridentifies a business and is specified via the DUNS number.
    • RosettaNet defines this entity as type Integer with length [9..9] and the representation 9(9).
    • In XSD, it is not possible to use the primitive type xsd:integer for this, as it does not allow the minLength=9 constraint to be expressed appropriately.
    • Therefore, we have chosen the XSD primitive type xsd:token together with length [9..9] and the additional XSD pattern \d+ (to ensure that only digits are permitted).  
  • Global Location Identifier
    • The GlobalLocationIdentifierdescribes a location uniquely identified by the DUNS+4 number.
    • In the majority of PIPs this entity is specified as type String with length [10..13] and the representation 9(9)4(X). However, a number of PIPs incorrectly use type Integer. 
    • In Integration Advisor, we consistently use type String together with length [10..13].  
  • Global Product Identifier
    • The GlobalProductIdentifier specifies a product identified by the Global Trade Identification Number (GTIN).
    • RosettaNet consistently defines this entity as type String with length [14..14] and the representation 9(14).
    • We represent this entity as type String together with length [14..14] as well, and include the representation 9(14) as part of the documentation. However, we have not added the additional XSD Pattern \d+ by default. (Unlike the Global Business Identifier, RosettaNet uses type String here, so we were not entirely sure whether the intention was to keep the option open for non-digit characters.)
    •  If you want to enforce that only digits shall be permitted, you can easily add the XSD pattern \d+ in your MIG. 

RosettaNet uses special date/time conventions, such as 20260618T114000.000Z. These are very similar to the standard XSD date and/or time conventions but differ in that hyphens and colons are omitted. We have included three additional Date Time Formats specific to RosettaNet and automatically assigned these patterns to the corresponding fields: pattern CCYYMMDD'T'hhmmss'.'fffZ for DateTimeStamp, pattern CCYYMMDDZ for DateStamp, and pattern hhmmss'.'fffZ for TimeStamp. In addition, we have added two more Date Time Formats to accommodate optional parts: pattern CCYYMMDD'T'hhmm[ss['.'fff]][Z] for DateTimeStamp (specified with length [13..20]) and pattern hhmm[ss['.'fff]][Z] for TimeStamp (specified with length [4..11]).

There is one minor limitation to note for FreeFormText: This field is specified with Min Length = 1 (but without Max Length) in the RosettaNet HTML Guidelines. In Integration Advisor, however, FreeFormText > CONTENT has no Min Length assigned to it.  (The reason for this is that FreeFormText is a so-called XSD Simple Content, which does not allow length specifications to be added without further modification of the XSD structure.) If this Min Length value is important for your use case, you can simply add it in your MIG. 

RosettaNet Usage in SAP Cloud Integration

Cloud Integration now supports the processing of RosettaNet messages. You can use the RNIF (RosettaNet Implementation Framework) adapter to exchange RosettaNet business messages with trading partners over HTTPS, in compliance with the RNIF 2.0 specification. The adapter supports both sender (inbound) and receiver (outbound) channels. For more information, refer to the Online Help.

For the runtime, one minor technical point is worth mentioning. Many RosettaNet payloads include a DOCTYPE declaration (such as <!DOCTYPE Pip3A4PurchaseOrderRequest SYSTEM "3A4_MS_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest.dtd">) at the beginning of the XML payload. The purpose of this is to allow payload validation against the underlying DTD schema. Integration Advisor and Cloud Integration, however, work with the newer XSD schema definition language. Such a DOCTYPE declaration does not interact well with XSD schema processing (e.g. in the XML Validator flow step). Therefore, DOCTYPE declarations are not part of the Integration Advisor processing and are automatically removed from the payload if present.

In Integration Advisor, each RosettaNet Message or MIG includes, for your reference, a documentation note (on the Notes tab) with the DTD file name (e.g. Original DTD file name: 3A4_MS_V02_02_PurchaseOrderRequest.dtd). This can be helpful if your business partner expects the DOCTYPE declaration to be set.

Conclusion

With this latest update, we now support the RosettaNet Message Standard. You have an end-to-end solution that allows you to view and customize RosettaNet messages in Integration Advisor and send and receive these messages in Cloud Integration.

1. HR Manager Role and Existing Relationships

You are absolutely right. As mentioned in the article, for this solution to work, the HR Manager role must not already be in use for another purpose.

However, during one of my tests, I created a rule to assign another user to the HR Manager role after the candidate had started employment. I did not encounter any issues that blocked the process in this scenario. While the recruiter continued to hold the HR Manager role throughout the recruitment process, another user could be assigned to this role after the candidate’s start date.

Therefore, although it remains important to review existing HR Manager relationships, this approach could be tested as an alternative solution.

2. Recruiter Changes and Onboarding Tasks

During my testing, I identified two possible solutions for situations where the recruiter changes after the candidate’s onboarding process has started:

  • Delegating tasks: When the recruiter changes, the user currently assigned to the tasks needs to delegate their tasks to another user.
  • Restarting the onboarding process: First, update the recruiter through the job requisition. Then, cancel the existing processes and initiate the onboarding process again.

These two approaches can be considered alternative ways to ensure that onboarding tasks are assigned to the appropriate users following a recruiter change.

Thank you for your valuable feedback and contributions.

entry.title: Re: IMPORT_UNEXPECTED_END_OF_DATA at start of update function module
entry.content:
Probably the type of the parameter in the function module is not the same type as the argument passed to this parameter.

For instance, the parameter type could be table instead of structure.

Because they are of different types, there's a failure in the internal call of IMPORT used by the kernel to pass the arguments of update function modules called in update task.

Sandra

entry.title: Re: Non-Mandatory Item Retraining Periods - SF Learning
entry.content:
Using two Curricula with the same Items in it for First Aid might be a solution for you.  If for instance if you are in Australia, then the Nationally Recognised course is "Provide First Aid" and is made up of the following nationally recognised units of competency:

  • - HLTAID011 Provide First Aid
  • - HLTAID010 Provide basic emergency life support
  • - HLTAID009 Provide cardiopulmonary resuscitation

So, if you created the following curricula:  CUR- Provide First Aid- REQUIRED

  • - HLTAID011 Provide First Aid
  • - HLTAID010 Provide basic emergency life support
  • - HLTAID009 Provide cardiopulmonary resuscitation

With the Initial Period set at "14 days", the Retraining Period of "1,095 days", and the Assignment Type as "Required" (aka Required = Yes).

Then assigned this curriculum by role specific Assignment Profile/s (or Manually) it would manage those employees that require this training for their roles. Showing them over due to complete the training and its expiry.

And a Second Curricula with all the same Items:  CUR- Provide First Aid- OPTIONAL

  • - HLTAID011 Provide First Aid
  • - HLTAID010 Provide basic emergency life support
  • - HLTAID009 Provide cardiopulmonary resuscitation

With "No" Initial Period set, the Retraining Period at "1,095 days", and the Assignment Type as "Optional" (aka Required = No).

And then assigned this curriculum by an Assignment Profiles that uses the "Item Completion" of any of the items it contains, then it would manage those employees that do not require this training for their roles but have completed this training.   As well as only showing the training of expired Items and not those that had not been ever attained (recorded) in their Items Completed.   

I hope that this solution gives you some options for how to manage this without any manual LMS Admin involvement?

Let us know if it helps or not and why not if it doesn't.

Cheers,

entry.title: Re: Building Your First Data Product in SAP Datasphere: Step-by-Step Practical Guide
entry.content:
Hi @igdulia ,

Thank you for your detailed question and for highlighting this important distinction.

In my example, I am using an SAP HANA Database (Disk and In-Memory) Space, not an SAP HANA Data Lake Files Space.

The guide focuses on creating a Marketplace Data Product in SAP Datasphere using the Data Sharing Cockpit.

For your scenario, I would recommend the following architecture:

1. Data Replication

Replicate the master data from SAP BW into local tables in an SAP HANA Database Space, including the Attribute and Text tables.

2. Dimension Modeling

Create Graphical Views to combine the relevant master data attributes and texts.

Set the appropriate semantic usage (Dimension), define the necessary keys and associations, and deploy the views. For multilingual texts, you can also consider separate Text entities with the corresponding associations.

3. SAP Analytics Cloud Consumption

Reuse these Dimensions in an Analytic Model by associating them with the relevant Fact entities.

The Analytic Model can then be consumed in SAP Analytics Cloud through a live connection.

One important distinction is that standalone Dimension Views are generally not consumed directly as live analytical models in SAC. They are typically reused within an Analytic Model.

4. Data Product Creation

If your requirement is to create a Marketplace Data Product within SAP Datasphere, you can reuse the same deployed Graphical Views.

Navigate to:

Data Sharing Cockpit → My Data Products → Create Data Product

  • Create a Data Product called BW Master Data.

  • Select your SAP HANA Database Space as the Artifact Space.

  • Add your deployed Graphical Views as Product Artifacts.

  • Configure the appropriate context and delivery mode.

  • Save and list the Data Product.

This allows multiple modeled Dimensions, such as Customer, Material, and Cost Center, to be included as artifacts in one Data Product.

5. When Would You Need an SAP HANA Data Lake Files Space?

This becomes relevant if you want to publish a custom Data Product for SAP Business Data Cloud using Delta Sharing.

In that case, the architecture is different because the supported artifacts are Local Tables (File), not Graphical Views.

You could follow this approach:

SAP BW → HANA Database Space → Graphical Views → Materialized Local Tables → HANA Data Lake Files Space → Local Tables (File) → BDC Data Product

The modeled results would need to be materialized and made available as Local Tables (File) in the Data Lake Files Space, for example through an appropriate sharing and transformation flow process.

Alternatively, if the BW data already resides in a File Space, you can use Spark Transformation Flows to prepare the output tables and share them with a HANA Database Space for analytical modeling.

My Recommendation

For your specific scenario, where the primary goal is to reuse business Dimensions in SAC while also publishing them as part of a Data Product, I would start with an SAP HANA Database Space.

You can maintain your business logic and semantic modeling in one place and reuse the deployed Views for the Marketplace Data Product.

Only introduce the HANA Data Lake Files layer if your requirement specifically includes publishing a Delta Share Data Product through SAP Business Data Cloud.

I hope this clarifies the difference between the two approaches and helps with your architecture decision.

Thank you again for raising this point. I will also make the Space type distinction clearer in the guide.

entry.title: iFlow Transport with Git and CI/CD – Setting Externalized Parameters with Automation Pilot
entry.content:
Introduction

Here are two recent updates around Cloud Integration:

  • July 2026: Cloud Integration can push iFlows to a Git repository and pull them from it.
  • September 2026: SAP Automation Pilot introduced the SAP Integration Suite (is-sapcp) catalog. It manages the lifecycle of iFlows, externalized parameters and the Partner Directory.

In addition, SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery (CI/CD) provides the SAP Integration Suite Artifacts 2.0 job. It takes an iFlow from a Git repository, uploads it to a target tenant and deploys it.

A possible next step would be to combine them: push an iFlow to Git, transport it to the target tenant with CI/CD, and then set the externalized parameters for that environment with Automation Pilot.

So I tried it. In this blog post, I will show how I connected these services and which gaps I had to bridge.

Note: I tested this on a BTP trial account. It is not a production-proven procedure.

Architecture

Figure: Overall architecture

  1. Develop the iFlow in the Dev tenant and push it to GitHub.
  2. Run the CI/CD job. It uploads the iFlow to the target tenant and deploys it.
  3. When the job succeeds, Alert Notification triggers an Automation Pilot command. The command sets the externalized parameters for the target environment and deploys them.

CI/CD deploys the iFlow, and Automation Pilot deploys only the externalized parameters.

Bridging the gaps

Gap 1: Repository structure

When Cloud Integration pushes an iFlow, it creates a folder named after the iFlow ID, so one repository can hold several iFlows. The CI/CD job, however, expects the content of one iFlow at the repository root.

# Pushed by Cloud Integration   # Expected by CI/CD
Test_Flow/                       META-INF/
├── META-INF/                    src/
├── src/                         metainfo.prop
└── metainfo.prop

As-is, the Upload stage fails with Integration flow project must contain a manifest file. The fix is one additional command in the Upload stage (Additional Commands > Run First in Stage). It zips the iFlow folder into the package.zip that the stage uploads:

python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.make_archive('package','zip','<iFlow ID>')"

Figure: Additional command in the Upload stage

Gap 2: Passing externalized parameters to Automation Pilot

The Automation Pilot command BulkPromoteIFlowToEnvironment takes the iFlow ID (iflowId) and the externalized parameters to set in the target environment (iflowParameters). The CI/CD Build Notification can carry such values in its Custom Tag:

Figure: Custom tag in the Build Notification settings

When Alert Notification triggers Automation Pilot, though, the whole event goes to the command as one input. The following JSON is the event (abbreviated). The custom tag is nested inside it as a JSON string:

{
  "eventType": "build.end",
  "subject": "Build has finished with 'SUCCESS'",
  "tags": {
    "cicd:custom": "{\"iflowId\": \"Test_Flow\", \"iflowParameters\": [{\"key\":\"header1\",\"value\":\"bulk\"}]}",
    "cicd:issuer": "SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery",
    "cicd:stage": "Integration Flow Result",
    ...
  },
  "resource": { "resourceType": "SAP Integration Suite Artifacts", ... },
  ...
}

So I created a small wrapper command, PromoteIFlowFromAnsEvent, with the help of SAP Automation Pilot Agent Skills. It receives the whole event as its payload input and runs two steps:

  1. customTag reads the cicd:custom tag from the event. If the tag has no iflowId, the command stops with an error message.
  2. promote calls BulkPromoteIFlowToEnvironment. It takes iflowId and iflowParameters from the custom tag (see the red boxes in the figure below), and the connection details of the target tenant from the command's input.

Figure: The promote step of the wrapper command

You can import the command from GitHub: https://github.com/miyasuta/automation-pilot-cicd-iflow

Configuration

Prerequisites:

  • A GitHub repository and a personal access token (PAT)
  • The following services in your subaccount:
    • SAP Integration Suite
    • SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery
    • SAP Alert Notification service
    • SAP Automation Pilot

1. Cloud Integration

Connect the repository and push the iFlow. See Integrating with GitHub and this blog post.

2. CI/CD

Set up an Integration Suite Artifacts 2.0 job as described in the documentation. Notes:

  • Create the integration package in the target tenant beforehand. CI/CD does not create it.
  • For Design Time Authentication, use a service key of SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api) in the target subaccount.
  • Additional settings for this scenario:
    • Upload > Additional Commands > Run First in Stage: Enter the zip command (Gap 1)
    • Build Notification: Turn on the notification, and enter the Alert Notification service key and the custom tag (Gap 2)

3. Automation Pilot

This step assumes that the wrapper command (Gap 2) already exists in your Automation Pilot tenant.

  1. Create an Input with the target tenant's credentials (clientId, clientSecret, tokenUrl, apiHost) from a service key of SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api).
  2. In Executions, click Build Event Trigger. Select the command and the input. On the Mapping tab, map the event to payload. Copy the event trigger URL.

Figure: Build Event Trigger, General tab

Figure: Build Event Trigger, Mapping tab

The SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api) service instances used by CI/CD and Automation Pilot have the following roles:

RoleCI/CDAutomation Pilot
WorkspacePackagesEdit✓✓
WorkspaceArtifactsDeploy✓✓
MonitoringDataRead✓✓
WorkspacePackagesConfigure ✓

Automation Pilot additionally needs WorkspacePackagesConfigure to update the externalized parameters.

4. Alert Notification

In Alert Notification, configure the following so that a successful CI/CD build triggers the Automation Pilot command:

  • Action: Create an action that calls the event trigger URL. Enter the username and password for the event trigger.
  • Conditions: Create two conditions so that only successful builds trigger the command: eventType equals build.end, and subject contains SUCCESS. For details of the event, see the event reference.
  • Subscription: Create a subscription that combines the action and both conditions.

Result

I ran the CI/CD job, and it finished successfully:

Figure: Successful CI/CD build

Alert Notification triggered the command:

Figure: Command execution in Automation Pilot

The externalized parameter has the value from the custom tag:

Figure: Externalized parameter set in the target tenant

Considerations

  • Single iFlows only. Both the Git integration and the CI/CD job handle individual iFlows. Scripts, value mappings and other artifacts in the package are not transported. If the iFlow depends on them, import the package to the target first.
  • One CI/CD job per iFlow and target environment. The number of jobs grows with the number of iFlows and environments. This setup can be an option for two-tier landscapes or a small number of iFlows. Otherwise, the standard approach is Cloud Transport Management with Content Assembly Service.

Summary

These services work well together. Only two small gaps had to be bridged: an additional zip command for the repository structure, and a wrapper command that extracts the externalized parameters from the Alert Notification event. With those, a single run of the CI/CD job transports an iFlow and sets its environment-specific parameters.
